stem: You work for an insurer whose recently deployed Gemini assistant summarizes claim notes for adjusters. After optimizing prompts, the service still omits required domain wording, and 5,000 approved prompt-and-summary pairs are already stored in BigQuery. You want to teach Gemini the desired summaries directly from that table by using SQL, evaluate the tuned result for this use case, and minimize data preparation and training-application development. What should you do?
correct_answer: Create a BigQuery ML remote model over a supported Gemini model, perform supervised tuning by selecting the prompt and label columns from the BigQuery table, and assess the tuned model with the EVALUATE function.
distractor_1: Keep the pretrained Gemini model and add several approved summaries to every prompt, then manually review a sample of its responses.
distractor_2: Export the prompt-and-summary pairs to a Cloud Storage dataset, start a supervised tuning job in Agent Platform Studio, and enable model validation.
distractor_3: Develop a custom training application for the summarization task and submit it through Agent Platform serverless training.
correct_explanation: The key constraints are to learn from the labeled examples already in BigQuery, use SQL, avoid developing a training application, and evaluate the result. BigQuery ML can create and train a remote model over a supported Gemini model through supervised tuning, with the training data supplied by a query that selects prompt and label columns. BigQuery ML then provides the EVALUATE function for assessing the tuned model. Prompting does not tune the model, Agent Platform Studio requires preparing a Cloud Storage dataset, and custom training requires application development and data preparation.
distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to teach Gemini from the labeled BigQuery table through supervised tuning. Prompt design uses instructions and examples without adapting the model, while supervised fine-tuning learns from labeled examples and is recommended when prompting does not resolve recurrent errors.
distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to use the existing BigQuery table directly through SQL while minimizing data preparation. Agent Platform Studio tuning takes a dataset file from Cloud Storage, whereas BigQuery ML can supply prompt and label columns directly from a BigQuery table when creating the tuned remote model.
distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize training-application development and data preparation. Agent Platform custom training requires programming, development of the training application, and handling data preparation. BigQuery ML instead uses SQL and the BigQuery computational engine for model training and evaluation.

stem: You work for an electronics manufacturer whose running Gemini 3 inspection system analyzes a close-up and a wider context photo for each circuit board. It still misses small solder defects, and using high resolution for every training image consumes too many tokens. You want to adapt the model to your labeled defect examples while minimizing image tokens without losing detail from the close-ups. What should you do?
correct_answer: Fine-tune Gemini with supervised learning. Use high media resolution for each close-up part and low global media resolution for the remaining images.
distractor_1: Fine-tune Gemini with supervised learning, but use low media resolution for every image in each training example.
distractor_2: Fine-tune Gemini with supervised learning, but use high media resolution for every image in each training example.
distractor_3: Replace the inspection model with an untuned Gemma model from Model Garden and deploy it to a GPU-backed endpoint using the default configuration.
correct_explanation: The system needs domain-specific image understanding, fine defect detail, and lower token use. Gemini supervised fine-tuning adapts a base model to visual-inspection tasks. Gemini 3 supports media resolution on individual image parts, and those part-level choices override the global choice. High resolution preserves more detail for close-ups, while low resolution uses fewer tokens for the other images. Using low resolution everywhere sacrifices detail, using high resolution everywhere does not minimize tokens, and deploying an untuned Model Garden model does not adapt the model to the labeled defects.
distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to preserve detail from the close-ups. Gemini image tuning uses fewer tokens at low media resolution, but higher resolution lets the model perceive more detail and can produce more nuanced tuned behavior.
distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize image tokens. Gemini image tuning uses more tokens at higher media resolution, while Gemini 3 allows individual image parts to use different resolutions.
distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to adapt the model to the company's labeled defect examples. Model Garden deployment places an open model on an endpoint for online predictions, while supervised fine-tuning is the Gemini capability that adapts a base model for specialized visual-inspection tasks.

stem: You lead machine learning for an online retailer whose nightly transformer training currently runs on CPU VMs and delays pricing updates. The team is migrating to either NVIDIA GPU or Google TPU clusters. Advertised peak specifications point in different directions, and the model might use each platform differently. You want to choose using the current model’s observed distributed-training performance while minimizing accelerator cost, and you want the comparison to expose efficiency losses as the cluster grows. What should you do?
correct_answer: Benchmark the same model on the smallest viable GPU and TPU clusters, compare tokens per second per chip and per dollar, and repeat the benchmark at increasing cluster sizes to measure scaling degradation.
distractor_1: Benchmark the same model on GPU and TPU clusters at increasing sizes, then select the platform with the highest raw tokens per second per chip.
distractor_2: Benchmark a GPU-optimized model on the GPU cluster and a TPU-optimized model on the TPU cluster, compare tokens per second per chip per dollar at several scales, and select the winner.
distractor_3: Run the current model on the smallest viable GPU and TPU clusters, compare tokens per second per chip per dollar, and select the platform with the better result.
correct_explanation: The decision has three constraints: use observed performance from the current model, account for accelerator cost, and reveal efficiency losses at larger scales. Model benchmarking on Compute Engine GPUs and TPUs measures real training throughput while holding the model architecture constant. Tokens per second per chip provides a normalized performance measure, and dividing it by chip cost produces tokens per second per chip per dollar. Repeating the benchmark at increasing cluster sizes shows how per-chip throughput degrades as the system scales. The alternatives omit cost normalization, change the model being compared, or test only one cluster size.
distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize accelerator cost. Tokens per second per chip measures normalized throughput, but the accelerator benchmarking methodology requires dividing that value by chip cost to compare performance per dollar. Raw performance can favor a faster chip even when another Compute Engine GPU or TPU provides better performance per dollar.
distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to evaluate the current model consistently across platforms. Accelerator comparisons for training should hold a specific representative model architecture constant. Models can be co-designed for particular hardware, so using a different optimized model for each Compute Engine GPU and TPU measures both model differences and hardware differences rather than the current model’s relative performance.
distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to expose efficiency losses as the cluster grows. A smallest-cluster benchmark establishes a baseline, but scaling degradation is evaluated by repeating the same model benchmark at larger chip counts and recalculating tokens per second per chip. A single Compute Engine GPU or TPU cluster size cannot reveal the distributed system’s scale tax.

stem: You work for a global publisher whose running localization pipeline extracts text from formatted word-processing and presentation documents, translates it, and has staff restore the original design. During migration to Google Cloud, nightly jobs will translate thousands of files from Cloud Storage into several languages. Approved product terms must remain consistent. You want each translation job to accept multiple documents and target languages while preserving layout and minimizing custom reconstruction and manual work. What should you do?
correct_answer: Partition the files into supported batch sizes and use Cloud Translation - Advanced batch Document Translation, applying the approved glossary and writing translated documents to Cloud Storage.
distractor_1: Call Cloud Translation - Advanced online Document Translation separately for every file and target language, applying the approved glossary to each request.
distractor_2: Use Document AI OCR to extract each document’s text and structure, translate the extracted text, and write application code that rebuilds every translated document.
distractor_3: Use Cloud Translation - Advanced batch Document Translation with the default Google-managed model, but omit the glossary and correct product terminology after translation.
correct_explanation: 1) The workload contains many formatted documents, several target languages, required terminology, and a need to retain layout. 2) Cloud Translation - Advanced batch Document Translation accepts multiple Cloud Storage files and multiple target languages in one request. Each request can contain up to 100 files, so the nightly workload should be partitioned into supported batches. 3) Document Translation preserves document formatting and layout, and its glossary support handles domain-specific terminology. 4) Online Document Translation handles only one file per request, Document AI OCR would leave the application to reconstruct translated documents, and omitting the glossary would not enforce the approved terms.
distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement that each translation job accept multiple documents and target languages. Cloud Translation - Advanced online Document Translation synchronously processes a single file with one target language, whereas batch Document Translation accepts multiple files and target languages in one request.
distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize custom layout reconstruction. Document AI OCR returns text and structural elements such as pages, blocks, paragraphs, lines, and tokens, but this approach explicitly requires application code to rebuild the output. Cloud Translation - Advanced Document Translation directly preserves much of the original formatting and layout.
distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to keep approved product terms consistent while minimizing manual work. Cloud Translation - Advanced supports applying a glossary to batch Document Translation for domain-specific terminology. Omitting it leaves the stated terminology policy to manual correction.
